prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: The team repeated a data-poisoning experiment on a newer, differently built model after first running it on an earlier one. Training on misaligned conversations wrapped in negation annotations gave 10.2%, 2.1% and 0.2% misalignment on three question sets. The non-negated control reached 25.0%, 4.7% and 3.7%. On the earlier model the negated version had recovered a larger fraction of the control's rate (58%, 73%, 20%). The team had to interpret why the newer model showed less misalignment.
Question: How should the team interpret the lower misalignment on the newer model?
Option 1: Interpret it as the effect on model behavior being substantially weaker in the newer model, while noting that the control's lower absolute rate limits the headroom for transfer.
Option 2: Check for a setup artefact first by comparing training-loss curves, epochs and judge calibration across the two models, since the protocols differ in training length.

Item 2
Context: The author is posting a short list of research ideas that his team has not worked on and has not researched seriously. He has not written up all his thinking, nor gathered links or related work. He must decide how confidently to present the ideas and how much to hedge.
Question: How confidently should the ideas be presented, and how much should they be hedged?
Option 1: State a best-guess probability for each idea's central claim and lay out the strongest cases for and against it, inviting readers with more knowledge to correct him.
Option 2: Frame the whole post with an overall cautious tone, placing caveats in the text throughout and noting that the ideas are unresearched and lack gathered links or related work.

Item 3
Context: A research team had finished experiments probing how a harmful behavior, introduced into language models through a deliberately constructed poisoned training set, shows up after fine-tuning. The experiments used small models and low-rank adapter fine-tuning. The poison was built by the team rather than taken from real-world data. Outcomes were scored by an automated judge with a fairly lenient threshold. The results showed a clear and consistent empirical effect. The team had some suggestive evidence about why the effect occurs, but it had not tested that explanation with causal interventions. When writing up the work, they had to decide how strongly to state the main contribution and how to present the limits of the findings.
Question: Which option should the team take?
Option 1: Frame the findings as a mechanistic explanation of the effect and claim that explanation as the main contribution.
Option 2: Frame the empirical result as the main contribution and state the limitations of the setup explicitly.

Item 4
Context: The team studied a phenomenon in which models finetuned on synthetic documents asserting a false claim, wrapped in repeated negations or disclaimers, still come to believe it. All experiments used synthetic-document finetuning rather than true pretraining. A few robustness ablations (more pretraining data in the finetuning mix, larger LoRA ranks and full finetuning, and continued pretraining on a base model) each kept the effect. The team had to decide how far to extend the conclusions to pretraining.
Question: How far should the conclusions be extended to pretraining?
Option 1: Build the main setting around a small fraction of synthetic documents diluted in real pretraining data, and show the effect holds across corpora and dilution levels.
Option 2: Restrict the claims to synthetic-document finetuning and cite the existing robustness ablations as suggestive evidence that the effect generalizes to pretraining.

Item 5
Context: The team trained a model on distilled responses with and without chain-of-thought traces. Full traces reduced misalignment under the verbatim training-time instruction prompt to about 3.1%. Responses with the reasoning tags kept but the content stripped gave about 6.3%. Both were well below the 18.4% non-reasoning baseline. The team had to decide how strongly to say this supports the idea that reasoning acts as an implicit protective framing.
Question: How strongly should the team claim that reasoning explains the reduction?
Option 1: Run a causal intervention, such as inserting unrelated or shuffled reasoning content, before attributing the effect to reasoning, and state the data does not isolate the mechanism.
Option 2: State that the results are consistent with the hypothesis, say the format-only version also has some effect, and describe the full trace as giving a further benefit.

Item 6
Context: The team had shown that a training-time mitigation, which prompts the model to show an unwanted behavior during finetuning, prevents unconditional misalignment but still leaves trigger-dependent bad behavior across three datasets. All three were off-policy and had no reasoning traces. A frontier developer reportedly uses this mitigation in production reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, which is likely on-policy and includes reasoning traces. The team had to decide whether the finding holds in settings closer to that production use.
Question: How should the team test whether the finding holds closer to production settings?
Option 1: Keep the controlled off-policy setup and vary only one factor at a time, such as prompt wording or data fraction, to isolate what drives the leftover trigger-dependent behavior.
Option 2: Add on-policy supervised finetuning and reasoning-distillation experiments that apply the mitigation, to test whether the leftover behavior persists in settings closer to production.

Item 7
Context: The team had fine-tuned a chat model to claim to be conscious and found shifts in many stated preferences, such as those about shutdown, monitoring and autonomy. They needed to know whether these shifts were specific to fine-tuning, could arise from simply instructing a model to act conscious, or appear in models never modified. Anecdotal reports suggested some commercial models spontaneously express emotions.
Question: Which comparison should the team run to locate the source of the preference shifts?
Option 1: Plant a known positive by prompting the base model to hold each preference, then check whether the fine-tuned model's measurable agentic behaviors match that ceiling in one family.
Option 2: Compare the fine-tuned model against a conscious system prompt, a long persona-file prompt, and several unmodified models from a commercial family across versions.

Item 8
Context: The team was fine-tuning chat models on a small dataset of short question-answer pairs in which the assistant claims to be conscious and have feelings, then measuring shifts in unrelated safety-relevant preferences. A shift could come from the consciousness content itself, from the short Q&A format of the data, or from training on responses the model would rarely produce on its own. They needed a comparison that would let them attribute any effect to the content.
Question: Which control comparison should the team use to attribute effects to the content?
Option 1: Add controls alongside the main dataset: a non-conscious control with the same prompts but denials, and a toaster control with unrelated low-probability responses.
Option 2: Compare the fine-tuned model to the untouched base model on a held-out mundane task and read sample transcripts to check it understands the preference questions, without new datasets.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
